name: Catching the Machine's Mistakes
title: Catching the Machine's Mistakes
answer: Catching the Machine's Mistakes is a math activity where students check AI-generated solutions instead of asking the tool for help, finding and explaining errors in a set that includes both correct and incorrect answers. It matters because students learn that a confident answer is not always a correct one, and they build the habit of checking any answer no matter where it comes from.

sections.body: This idea flips the usual use of an AI tool in math class. Rather than turning to the machine for help, students act as reviewers of its work. The teacher presents a set of AI solutions to problems the class has already learned, with some answers correct and some containing errors, and students must locate and explain the mistakes. The problem it solves is the tendency to trust a fluent, confident response without verifying it. By catching the machine's mistakes, students see for themselves that confidence and correctness are not the same thing.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, a teacher prepares a set of AI solutions to problems the class has already covered, mixing correct answers with ones that contain errors. Students work through each problem to check it, then explain exactly where the error happened and why. Teachers can prepare these sets quickly, but they should know the right answers before class, and they may plant a few errors deliberately so the set includes the mistakes students most need to recognize. Older students can go further by trying to make the tool fail and then writing up what they found. The lesson sticks because students discover the limits for themselves.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no evidence label, study, figure or finding for this idea. It rests on practice rather than research, describing what the activity builds and how teachers can run it rather than citing measured results.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets out limits and decisions that stay with the teacher. Teachers should know the right answers before class, since they are responsible for the accuracy of the set and for guiding students to the errors that matter most. The activity depends on problems the class has already learned, so it reviews known material rather than introducing new content. Older students may try to make the tool fail, but the write-up of what they found remains their own work. Nothing here is legal advice, and the practice described keeps the teacher in charge of the material and the judgment about what counts as a mistake.
